'''''Cleomella arborea'''''<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Patchell |first=Melanie J. |last2=Roalson |first2=Eric H. |last3=Hall |first3=Jocelyn C. |date=2014-04-01 |title=Resolved phylogeny of Cleomaceae based on all three genomes |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.12705/632.17 |journal=Taxon |language=en |volume=63 |issue=2 |pages=315–328 |doi=10.12705/632.17|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Roalson |first=Eric H. |last2=Hall |first2=Jocelyn C. |last3=Riser II |first3=James P. |last4=Cardinal-McTeague |first4=Warren M. |last5=Cochrane |first5=Theodore S. |last6=Sytsma |first6=Kenneth J. |date=2015-04-21 |title=A revision of generic boundaries and nomenclature in the North American cleomoid clade (Cleomaceae) |url=https://biotaxa.org/Phytotaxa/article/view/phytotaxa.205.3.1 |journal=Phytotaxa |volume=205 |issue=3 |pages=129 |doi=10.11646/phytotaxa.205.3.1 |issn=1179-3163|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name = powo /> is a [[perennial plant|perennial]] shrub or bush in the spiderflower family ([[Cleomaceae]]) known by the common names '''bladderpod''', '''bladderpod spiderflower''', and '''burro-fat'''.<ref name="Jepson">{{Jepson eFlora |first1=Robert E. |last1=Preston |first2=Staria S. |last2=Vanderpool |date=2023|id=101653 |taxon=Cleomella arborea|access-date=2024-11-18}}</ref><ref name="PLANTS">{{cite PLANTS | symbol=CLIS | date= 2018 | taxon= Cleome isomeris | access-date= 2018-07-06}}</ref><ref name=MDW>{{Cite book
| last1     = MacKay | first1 = Pam
| title     = Mojave Desert Wildflowers
| year      = 2013
| publisher = [[FalconGuides]]
| location  = Guilford, Connecticut
| page      = 230
| isbn      = 978-0762780334
| language  = en
}}</ref><ref name=FNA>{{Cite eFloras|1|250094759|Peritoma arborea| first1=Staria S. |last1=Vanderpool |first2=Hugh H. |last2=Iltis |date=2010|access-date= 2018-07-18}}</ref> It grows up to 0.5 - 2 meters (1ft 8in -6ft 7in) high. It stems are densely branching and covered in tiny hairs. Leaves are typically composed of three equal leaflets, 15-45mm long, oval to elliptic, and pointed.

The plant produces bright yellow flowers nearly year-round. Each flower has four petals (8-14 mm long) and six producing stamens. The fruit is a leathery capsule, 30-60mm long, which matures from green to light brown. <ref name="MDW" /> The plant produces a strong odor that likely deters insects from feeding on it.<ref name="FNA" /> 

==Range and habitat==
''Cleomella arborea'' is commonly found along roadsides, [[desert dry wash]]es, and flat areas up to {{Convert|4200|feet|-2}} in the western [[Mojave Desert]] and [[Colorado Desert]] to the [[Baja California Peninsula]].<ref name="Sullivan2018"/><ref name=MDW/> It is native to [[California]] and the Baja California Peninsula where it grows in a variety of habitats usually described as desert or brush.<ref name="Sullivan2018">{{cite web | url= http://www.wildflowersearch.com/search?&PlantName=Peritoma+arborea | last= Sullivan | first= Steven. K. | date= 2018 | title= ''Peritoma arborea'' | website= Wildflower Search | access-date= 2018-07-06}}</ref>

[[File:Peritoma_arborea_8240.JPG|thumb|left|A typical individual bears flowers and fruit in various stages of development.]]

==Description==
It is a densely branching [[shrub]] {{Convert|0.5|-|2|m}} high covered with tiny hairs.<ref name="Jepson"/><ref name=MDW/> Its stalked leaves are generally composed of three equal leaflets {{Convert|15|-|45|mm|1}} long, oval to elliptic in shape and pointed at the tip.<ref name="Jepson"/><ref name=MDW/> The plant produces abundant [[inflorescence]]s at the ends of the stem branches much of the year.<ref name=MDW/> The four [[sepal]]s are fused about halfway from their base.  Each flower has four bright yellow {{Convert|8|-|14|mm|1}} long petals, six protruding {{Convert|15|-|25|mm|1}} [[stamen]]s with {{Convert|2|-|2.5|mm|1}} [[anther]]s.<ref name="Jepson" /> The style is {{Convert|0.9|-|1.2|mm|2}} or aborts before flowering.<ref name="Jepson"/> The fruit is a leathery prolate spheroid capsule {{Convert|30|-|60|mm|1}} long and {{Convert|10|-|25|mm|1}} wide on a {{Convert|10|-|20|mm|1}} stalk. It is smooth and green when new, aging to light brown.<ref name="Jepson"/>

A typical inflorescence bears a number of flower buds at its tip, open flowers proximal to the buds, and maturing fruits which have shed their flowers below these.

In the previous genus name, ''Isomeris'', "''iso''" means "equal", and "''meris''" means "part", referring to the stamens being of equal length.<ref>Torrey, J. & A. Gray. A flora of North America. 1838 [-1840]. volume 1.page 124.[https://biodiversitylibrary.org/page/5290592]</ref>

== Ecology ==
Blooming throughout the year, ''C. arborea'' provides a nectar source for pollinators such as bees and butterflies. The plant is adapted to arid environments and tolerates dry soil and conditions.

== Ethnobotany ==
[[File:Cleome_isomeris_(or_Peritoma_arborea)_(27374076351).jpg|thumb|244x244px|Desirable parts of the plant chosen for consumption were flowers (pictured to the left) and the pea pods (pictured to the right).]]
Various parts of bladderpod have been used by many tribes indigenous to California and Baja California. The seeds and flowers were eaten by the Diegueño (former Spanish name for [[Kumeyaay]]) and [[Kawaiisu]] tribes.<ref>Smither-Kopperl, M. 2012. [https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/plantmaterials/capmcpg11060.pdf Plant Guide for bladderpod (''Peritoma arborea'')]. USDA-Natural Resources Conservation Service, and Lockeford Plant Materials Center, Lockeford, CA 95237</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Hinton |first=Leanne |date=1975 |title=Notes on La Huerta Diegueño Ethnobotany |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/27824840 |journal=The Journal of California Anthropology |volume=2 |issue=2 |pages=214–222 |issn=0361-7181}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Zigmond |first=Maurice L. |title=Kawaiisu ethnobotany |date=1981 |publisher=Univ. of Utah Pr |isbn=978-0-87480-132-3 |location=Salt Lake City}}</ref> The tribes would boil the gathered plants to remove any bitter taste.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> The Kawaiisu tribe also prepared the flowers by cooking them in the dirt with hot rocks overnight until flowers turned red.<ref name=":1" /> The [[Cahuilla]] tribes prepared the pods in a similar fashion as the Kawaiisu; they cooked immature pods in the ground using hot stones.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Barrows |first=David Prescott |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/bibliography/19178 |title=The ethno-botany of the Coahuilla Indians of Southern California ... |date=1900 |publisher=University of Chicago Press |location=Chicago |doi=10.5962/bhl.title.19178}}</ref> The Kumeyaay preferred to consume the flowers of the plant rather than the leaves or pods.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Wilken |first=Michael Alan |url=https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/dam/sdc/pds/ceqa/JVR/AdminRecord/IncorporatedByReference/Appendices/Appendix-E---Cultural-Resources-Report/Wilken%202012_Ethnobotany%20of%20Baja%20California.pdf |title=An Ethnobotany of Baja California's Kumeyaay Indians |publisher=San Diego State University |year=2012 |location=San Diego |pages=104-105}}</ref> After cooking, they ate the flowers alone or with other ingredients, commonly eaten alongside [[tortilla]]s or [[Wiiwish|acorn mush]].<ref name=":2" /> 

The immature pea pods of the plant resemble garden peas and are edible small quantities; they may be used similarly to [[caper]]s.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Bladderpod |url=https://www.onceuponawatershed.org/bladderpod#:~:text=Some%20Native%20Americans%20relished%20the,can%20be%20used%20as%20capers. |access-date=2024-11-18 |website=onceuponawatershed |language=en}}</ref> Cooking was often used to remove the bitter characteristics of the plant which derive from [[glucocapparin]].<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bell |first=Luke |last2=Oloyede |first2=Omobolanle O. |last3=Lignou |first3=Stella |last4=Wagstaff |first4=Carol |last5=Methven |first5=Lisa |date=2018-03-26 |title=Taste and Flavor Perceptions of Glucosinolates, Isothiocyanates, and Related Compounds |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mnfr.201700990 |journal=Molecular Nutrition & Food Research |language=en |volume=62 |issue=18 |doi=10.1002/mnfr.201700990 |issn=1613-4125}}</ref> Flowers were commonly eaten alone or with tortillas or acorn mush. {{-}}
